child_drafts.description_long: At a February 12, 2026 event hosted by the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum called the energy transition an ideological “fantasy” and questioned climate projections. E&E News reported that he described climate forecasts as based on incomplete data and likened belief in the transition to a “semi-religion.” The article also records his comments on the administration’s planned critical-mineral reserve, Project Vault: Burgum suggested that it might expand if market demand justified more investment. E&E News situated the speech on the same day the administration announced repeal of the EPA endangerment finding, a policy that had underpinned rules limiting greenhouse-gas emissions. Those details describe the remarks and their reported policy context; they do not establish that the speech itself changed climate policy or authorized a lease. The NPR-A auction took place separately on March 18, 2026, so its bid totals and acreage belong in a distinct event record.

child_drafts.description_long: On March 18, 2026, the Interior Department held an oil and gas lease sale in the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska. The department reported that 11 companies bid on 187 of the 625 tracts offered, covering about 1.335 million acres, and that the sale generated $163,696,722 in receipts. Interior called it the reserve’s highest-revenue sale, the sale with the most tracts receiving bids, and the second-largest by acreage. It was the first NPR-A sale since 2019 and the first under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Interior stated that Alaska would receive nearly $82 million, half the receipts, with some proceeds benefiting North Slope communities. The same release describes other administration actions affecting the reserve, including rescinding the 2024 leasing rule and adopting an activity plan reopening nearly 82 percent of the reserve to leasing. Those actions provide context but are distinct from this single-day auction. The page does not support the original card’s unrelated royalty-rate or congressional-criticism claims.

remaining_gap: The original card’s additional claims about reduced royalty rates, congressional criticism, and simultaneous EPA climate deregulation are not part of either sourced event draft and need separate evidence or omission.

corrected_draft.title: Trump says he will always abide by courts during funding-freeze case
corrected_draft.description_short: Trump told ABC News he would “always abide by the courts” as an appeals court rejected an emergency request in the funding-freeze dispute.
corrected_draft.description_medium: On February 11, 2025, President Donald Trump told ABC News he would “always abide by the courts” as a federal appeals court considered the administration’s challenge to a lower-court order blocking a broad funding freeze. The First Circuit denied an immediate request to pause that order and left the district court to clarify its scope. The remark does not support the held claim that Trump said he could override court
corrected_draft.description_long: On February 11, 2025, President Donald Trump told ABC News he would “always abide by the courts” during a dispute over the administration’s effort to freeze federal funding. That day, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit denied the administration’s request for an immediate administrative stay of a lower-court order blocking the broad freeze. The appellate panel said it was uncertain what standards governed the requested stay and noted that the administration had not cited authority supporting it. The court left the district judge to clarify the scope of the earlier order and said it would consider a later request for a stay pending appeal. ABC reported that the administration argued the order improperly constrained executive spending authority, while state plaintiffs said a renewed freeze would harm recipients of federal funding. Trump’s brief assurance was made in this litigation context. It contradicts the held card’s claim that he declared he was not bound by court orders; the evidence supports recording the February statement and court response, not the alleged March declaration.

corrected_draft.description_short: Attorney General Pam Bondi created a Justice Department working group to review Trump-related investigations, including state investigations in New York.

corrected_draft.description_long: On February 5, 2025, Attorney General Pam Bondi created a Justice Department “Weaponization Working Group” to review what she described as politicized justice. The Washington Post reported that the group would begin with federal criminal cases brought against Donald Trump by special counsel Jack Smith. Bondi also ordered an examination of alleged federal cooperation in Trump’s New York criminal and civil investigations, which were conducted by state authorities, including Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg. The report separately describes acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove’s personnel actions and review of roughly 5,000 FBI agents who had worked on January 6 cases. Those were separate directives and should not be folded into a claim that DOJ opened a criminal investigation of Bragg. The article documents a review directive, not a criminal probe into the Manhattan DA, and does not establish that the federal review produced charges or findings against him.

remaining_gap: A source establishing a distinct DOJ criminal investigation of Bragg was not found; this supported February 5 review directive is a narrower, separate event.

corrected_draft.title: Trump threatens to revoke Harvard’s tax-exempt status
corrected_draft.description_short: Trump said his administration would revoke Harvard’s tax-exempt status; Harvard called the threat unlawful and unprecedented.

Reuters described the statement as a renewed threat after a similar post on April 15. Harvard called revocation unlawful and unprecedented. The university was already challenging a federal freeze of about $2.2 billion in grants, most of which supported medical and scientific research. corrected_draft.description_long: On May 2, 2025, President Donald Trump posted that his administration would take away Harvard University’s tax-exempt status. Reuters reported that Trump gave no explanation in that post and described it as a renewed threat following a similar statement on April 15. Harvard responded that revocation would be unlawful and unprecedented, and said there was no legal basis to rescind its status. At the time, Harvard was already suing over a federal freeze of about $2.2 billion in grants, most of which supported medical and scientific research. Reuters also reported that the university had faced demands concerning governance, faculty and student viewpoints, masks, and diversity initiatives after rejecting the administration’s terms. The article distinguishes Trump’s threat from an actual IRS revocation: IRS representatives did not respond to Reuters’ questions, and the White House said any IRS action would be independent. The record should therefore describe a public threat directed at Harvard on May 2, not a completed tax-status change or a February action against multiple universities.

remaining_gap: The original February date and multi-university scope are unsupported; the supported Harvard threat is dated May 2, 2025.
